en.text: Sexual propagation raises plants from seed. A seed has a protective seed coat, an endosperm food reserve and an embryo, the young plant. Pre-sowing treatments such as soaking in hot or cold water, heating, soaking in chemicals or alternate wetting and drying break seed dormancy. Seed propagation is cheap and gives hardy, long-lived trees and rootstocks, but seedlings bear late, grow large and are not guaranteed true to type. A nursery soil mix is forest soil, sand and farmyard manure in the ratio 2:1:1.

ideas.name: Asexual propagation: cuttings and air layering

en.text: Asexual (vegetative) propagation uses leaves, stems or roots; the new plants are exact copies of the mother plant, and because the material comes from an adult plant they have no juvenile phase. Methods include cuttings, air layering, grafting, budding and micro propagation. A stem cutting 15–30 cm long, with lower leaves, fruits and buds removed, is dipped in rooting hormone and set in a moist medium. In air layering a branch forms adventitious roots while still attached, then is cut off and planted.

en.text: Grafting joins parts of plants so they unite and grow as a single plant: the scion becomes the top (canopy) and the rootstock gives the roots. Cleft or wedge grafting is the most common field method. Stock and scion must be compatible, usually the same or closely related species. The cambial regions must touch, the union is held tight and sealed with wax or tape, shoots from the stock are removed, and the knife is kept razor sharp. Avocado is commercially grafted onto seedling rootstocks.

screens.title: Grafting
paras: Grafting joins plant parts so they grow as one plant.
Scion: the upper part, the canopy.
Stock or rootstock: the lower part with the roots.
Cleft (wedge) grafting is the most common field method.
Stock and scion must be compatible or they will not unite.
Use the same species or closely related species.
Avocado is grafted onto seedling rootstocks.
screens.note: The book says "closely related species or plant families". A whole family is too broad; grafts usually work within a species or genus.

screens.title: Requirements for success
paras: Cambial regions of scion and stock touch closely.
Choose healthy, strong, pest-free stock and scion.
Hold the cut surfaces tightly.
Cover the union with wax, tape or moist material.
Care for the graft until it unites.
Remove shoots from the stock.
Tie vigorous scion shoots.
Keep the knife razor sharp.

screens.title: Wedge (V) grafting
steps: Cut the base of the scion into a V-shaped wedge.
Split the rootstock down the middle.
Insert the wedge so the cambial regions touch.
Tie the union tightly with string.
Wrap the union fully with tape.

notes.text: p.29: "genetic purity" is defined backwards ("the degree of contamination"); the lesson defines it as freedom from other varieties or species.

p.30: apples are normally propagated by grafting or budding, not cuttings (cuttings root poorly). "apportion" should be "a portion". p.31: the Adventitious root key-term box is cut off; completed as "not from the primary root of the seed".
p.31: air-layering examples are ornamentals; Figure 2.4 shows ground (stool) layering, not air layering. p.32: grafting "within plant families" is too broad (same species or genus).
Figure 2.3 is used twice (seeds p.28, cuttings p.30), and the p.28 photo shows whole fruits, not seeds. Budding and micro propagation are named but never described.
Added (marked): the 2:1:1 mixing worked example and items, how air layering is done, fruit examples for air layering.
